summary:
Analog Earth: A Global Scan for Lunar and Martian Landing Zones

We built an interactive 3D globe that identifies lesser-known terrestrial analogs for the Artemis lunar south pole and Mars landing zones. Using Python in Google Colab, we scanned 204 global land cells against planetary reference profiles. Our tool pulls live climate data from the NASA POWER API (minimum temperature, temperature range, precipitation, surface pressure) and terrain roughness from Open-Meteo.

The 3D globe displays a continuous interpolated heatmap rather than scattered pins. Users can toggle between Moon and Mars targets, adjust weighting sliders to re-rank global sites in real-time, and hide well-known analogs (like Antarctica and the Atacama) to reveal lesser-studied candidates such as those in Siberia or the Tibetan Plateau.

As the challenge requires, clicking any region shows a breakdown of what matches and explicitly where the analogy fails—noting that Earth cannot replicate 1/6 gravity, hard vacuum, or cosmic radiation. This tool gives mission planners a fast, data-driven method to find accessible new test environments for rover mobility and hardware survival.
details:
Project Title

Analog Earth: A Global Scan for Lunar and Martian Landing Zones

The Challenge

"Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars."
Future mission planners need terrestrial environments to test hardware, rovers, and habitats before launching. While famous analogs like the Atacama Desert exist, we need a systematic way to discover new, lesser-known sites and explicitly understand where those analogies fail.

The Solution

We built an interactive, live 3D globe that visualizes a planet-wide environmental scan. Instead of dropping arbitrary pins, our tool processes a 10° grid of 204 global land cells, compares them to planetary targets, and generates a continuous, interpolated heatmap directly onto the continents.

How It Works (Technical Details)

  1. Data Collection: We used Python in Google Colab to pull live data using the NASA POWER API (minimum temperature, daily temperature range, precipitation, and surface pressure). We also used Open-Meteo to calculate terrain roughness (standard deviation of elevation).
  2. Scoring Engine: Each cell is scored against a reference profile using a weighted similarity algorithm (1 minus the normalized difference).
  3. Interactive Interface: The frontend is built using globe.gl to render a 3D interactive globe.

Key Features

  • Dual Targets: A toggle allows users to switch between a Lunar South Pole profile (-230°C, no atmosphere) and a Mars profile (-100°C, 0.6 kPa CO₂ atmosphere).
  • Dynamic Re-ranking: Users can move sliders to adjust the weight of different traits (e.g., prioritizing surface pressure for Mars, or sun angle for the Moon) and watch the global map recalculate in real-time.
  • Finding the Unknown: A dedicated "Hide well-known analogs" checkbox removes heavily studied regions like Antarctica, the Atacama, and Iceland. This forces the tool to highlight overlooked candidates, such as Siberia, the Tibetan Plateau, and the Arctic.
  • Live Precision: A "Top %" slider allows researchers to filter out weak matches, shading only the most promising regions.

Where the Analogy Breaks Down

The challenge explicitly asked to explain what doesn't match. Our tool addresses this in the detail panel:

  • Clicking any region provides a breakdown table comparing Earth data to the planetary target.
  • It explicitly states physical limitations: No Earth location can replicate 1/6 (or 0.38) gravity, a hard vacuum, or the cosmic radiation environment.
  • It identifies the "strongest" and "weakest" matches for every specific cell.

Conclusion

By combining NASA climate APIs with a 3D spatial interface, "Analog Earth" transforms a massive global dataset into a practical mission-planning dashboard. It allows researchers to discover cost-effective, accessible Earth environments for rover mobility testing, battery survival, and ISRU (In-Situ Resource Utilization) preparation.
